$comment: Dev-tree advisories that have been looked at and accepted for now. Read by
scripts/check-audit.mjs; anything not listed here fails the supply-chain job.
Rules: `id` is the GHSA identifier, not the npm advisory number. `why` is
the actual reasoning, not a restatement of the title. `expires` is the date
the decision stops being valid, after which the gate fails until somebody
looks again — an allow-list without expiry dates is just a mute button.
There is no equivalent file for the production tree. An advisory that can
reach a user is a release decision and has no allow-list.
Note that `npm audit`'s headline count is packages, not advisories: it said
6 on 2026-08-12 while there were 7 distinct GHSAs, because three separate
vite advisories collapse into one line of its human-readable output.
Four of those seven — the three vite advisories and the nested esbuild one —
were removed on 2026-08-16 because they were fixed, not because they lapsed.
`overrides.vite` in package.json pins vite ^6.4.3 under vitepress, which
carries esbuild ^0.25. The reasoning is in ADR-0005's amendment; the lesson
is that a transitive advisory has two escape routes, and the first pass only

allowed.why: Reached only through mocha, which pins diff@^7 and has no fixed release: mocha@11.8.0 is the latest stable and mocha 12 is at rc.6. `npm audit fix --force` proposes mocha@11.3.0, which is a downgrade from what is installed and fixes nothing. A denial of service in patch parsing, in a test runner, on input that is our own test files.

Same dependency path and the same absence of a fix: mocha pins serialize-javascript@^6.0.2 and the fixed line is 7.x. RCE via crafted RegExp flags, exploitable only by whoever controls the values being serialised — here, mocha serialising our own test results. Rated high on the general case, not on this one.
Second advisory against the same package on the same unfixable mocha path. CPU exhaustion while serialising array-likes we author ourselves.
